entities.summary:
Philippe de Luxembourg (died 1519), a scion of the powerful House of Luxembourg-Ligny, emerged as a cardinal and influential prelate within the late 15th and early 16th-century French ecclesiastical and political landscape. His career spanned the reigns of Charles VIII and Louis XII, placing him at the intersection of French monarchical ambition and papal authority. As a cardinal-bishop, he wielded significant spiritual and temporal power, reflecting the intricate connections between noble lineage, church office, and statecraft in Western Europe during the transition from the Medieval to the early Modern era. His life's trajectory, marked by rapid ascent, exemplifies the system of patronage and dynastic influence prevalent in the pre-Reformation Catholic Church.

Elevated to Bishop of Le Mans in 1476, Philippe de Luxembourg's ecclesiastical career advanced swiftly, culminating in his creation as a cardinal by Pope Alexander VI in 1495. He subsequently held multiple bishoprics, including Thérouanne (1503) and Arras (1516), often concurrently, demonstrating the accumulation of benefices common among high-ranking clergy of the period. His diplomatic skills were frequently employed by the French crown; he served as a trusted advisor to King Louis XII, representing French interests within the College of Cardinals and at various papal courts. A notable engagement was his participation in the controversial Council of Pisa (1511), convened by Louis XII against Pope Julius II, and subsequently his alignment with the Fifth Lateran Council (1512–1517), which aimed at Church reform and reconciliation.
